QF.id: AIFM Fee Structure and Fund Performance_71

question.text: Shanti Equity Opportunity Fund (open-ended Cat III) experiences a 20% drawdown. The IM wants to reset HWM to current NAV. What is the CORRECT governance procedure?

answer.text: Reset unilaterally — IM has fee-setting discretion
Reset only for new Class B investors entering post-drawdown
Seek LPAC/majority investor consent AND disclose the reset in LP communication; amend PPM if required

explanation.text: The Logic: The High-Water Mark is a fee-protective benchmark for investors: performance fees apply only on returns above the prior HWM, so resetting it lower transfers economic value from existing LPs to the manager. Because of that conflict, any reset is governed by the fund documents and is typically not unilateral — it is sought via LPAC and/or majority investor consent, accompanied by clear LP disclosure, and a corresponding PPM amendment where required. The Trap: Unilateral reset (A) ignores manager fiduciary duty. Class-specific reset for new Class B investors (B) creates discriminatory treatment that runs counter to standard MFN/fair-treatment principles. An "automatic SEBI reset" (C) is fictional — SEBI does not auto-reset HWM after a drawdown. Note: The specific HWM-reset governance procedure (LPAC/majority-investor consent plus PPM amendment) is not stated in the cited workbook chapter (FINAL_Series-XIX-C_AIF Managers_Ver-Dec-2025.pdf, pp. 155-159, 432-433, 500-505), which covers HWM purpose and disclosure but not reset mechanics. The framing above is general industry/governance practice for HWM amendments.
